title: Go and See for Yourself
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien's back-to-school open letter to school leaders argues that the single most reliable instructional-leadership axiom is Taiichi Ohno's genchi genbutsu, 'go and see for yourself,' applied specifically to student work rather than to walking classrooms and watching teacher delivery. He recounts Ohno's practice of chalking a circle on the Toyota factory floor and having managers stand in it for hours simply observing the actual work, arguing schools have an equivalent 'circle': the student's notebook, worksheet, or exit ticket, which he calls the only artifact in a building with no incentive to be optimistic. O'Brien contrasts this with the proxies leaders typically rely on instead, test scores (which describe last spring, not now), walkthrough impressions of teacher delivery, and dashboards, arguing all of them are commentary on the work rather than the work itself. He admits his own past failure mode as a former principal: years of observations that could describe a teacher's pacing and routines in detail while telling him nothing about what any individual child had actually written down. The piece closes with a concrete operational ask, not for the first chaotic week of school but for the weeks after, to schedule a defended, recurring time each week to examine real student work with a coalition of colleagues who can act on what they find.
points: Adapts Taiichi Ohno's Toyota Production System practice of genchi genbutsu ('go and see for yourself') into a school-leadership axiom: examine student work directly rather than relying on proxies.

Explicitly ranks common leadership data sources as inferior proxies: test scores describe last spring, walkthroughs capture teacher delivery rather than student thinking, and dashboards show altitude without explaining cause.

Admits a personal past failure mode: years of classroom observations that could describe a teacher's pacing and routines in detail while revealing nothing about what any individual student had actually written.
Recommends a concrete operational practice: a defended, recurring weekly time slot to examine real student work with a coalition of colleagues empowered to act on the findings.
quotes: Culture needs a minute to set. Nerves need a minute to settle. Nobody does deep strategic work in the first five days, and any leader who tells you they do is either lying or has a very generous definition of strategy.
He called it genchi genbutsu. Go and see for yourself. That's your axiom.
Go see the student work for yourself because the student work is the truth.
Test scores tell you what happened last spring, which is useful if you own a time machine. Surveys tell you how people feel about what happened.
Conviction is believing the student work over the teacher practice especially when the delivery is pretty darn good. Discipline is looking anyway.
Data without reteach is documentation. Looking at student work and changing nothing is worse than not looking, because now you've seen it and you're choosing.
